strengths: Addresses an important robotics problem through a coherent combination of spatially grounded reasoning, embodiment-independent visual guidance, and robot execution.

Reports encouraging results across several established benchmarks, including 80.9% on CVBench, 63.3% on EmbSpatial, and 56.7% on RoboRefIt. Evaluation extends beyond perception to simulation and physical robot experiments.

The hierarchical annotation pipeline and VABench could be useful resources. Table 3 provides initial evidence for SrCoT, with point accuracy increasing from 26.21% without SrCoT to 61.82% with the full method.
weaknesses: The central simulation result is internally inconsistent. Table 4 lists FSD task success rates of 41.6%, 50.0%, 33.3%, and 37.5%, averaging approximately 40.6%, not the repeatedly claimed 54.1%. With equal episode counts, the displayed results place FSD below SpatialVLA (FT) at 42.7%, contradicting the claimed best average performance. This discrepancy materially undermines the main robotics conclusion.

Zero-shot generalization is insufficiently established. Training uses BridgeData, RT-X, and DROID, while VABench draws from overlapping dataset sources and SimplerEnv evaluates related manipulation settings. Episode, scene, object, and task disjointness are not documented. Section 3.3 also describes iteratively refining filters against manually annotated test sets without clarifying whether these are separate development sets.

The execution method leaves a critical geometric issue unresolved: back-projecting predicted image waypoints using observed depth yields visible surface locations, not necessarily the intended free-space trajectory of a lifted object. The paper does not adequately specify intermediate waypoint depths, orientations, grasp-to-object offsets, or trajectory optimization constraints. Consequently, the claimed conversion from 2D reasoning to feasible SE(3) motion is difficult to assess.

Comparisons do not isolate the proposed reasoning contribution. FSD uses depth, GraspNet or predetermined grasps, and motion planning, whereas simulation VLA results are imported from another paper without establishing equivalent sensing and execution conditions. Physical baselines are restricted to start/end points, disadvantaging them on trajectory-dependent tasks. Controlled comparisons with the same executor and relevant hierarchical methods such as HAMSTER or ReKep are missing.

Novelty and component attribution remain limited. Visual trajectories, spatial affordances, grounded CoT, and inverse instruction prediction build on established ideas. The ablations do not disentangle spatial graph anchoring from generic CoT, additional supervision, or the training curriculum, and there are no robot-success ablations. The alignment improvement in trajectory GPT Score is only 5.45 to 5.49, without uncertainty estimates.

VABench validation is incomplete. The 300 problems lack documented split construction, annotation agreement, and judge calibration. Distance to a single reference trajectory can penalize alternative valid paths, while the GPT-based score is not validated against human judgments or execution success. The principal external trajectory baseline is a DINOv2 predictor rather than a comparably pretrained, language-conditioned model.

Reproducibility and statistical support are inadequate in the supplied manuscript. Appendices A–J are repeatedly cited but absent from the 14-page PDF, leaving training hyperparameters, data mixtures, prompts, filtering rules, execution details, and evaluation protocols unavailable. Real-world trial counts and confidence intervals are unspecified, and the simulation evaluation provides only 24 episodes per task without uncertainty estimates.

strengths: FSD addresses a meaningful robotics problem through a coherent combination of spatially grounded reasoning, embodiment-independent visual guidance, and a hierarchical training-data pipeline.

The spatial-understanding results are promising: FSD improves over its ASMv2 backbone across the reported benchmarks, achieves 56.7% on RoboRefIt versus RoboPoint’s 49.8%, and remains competitive on Where2Place.

VABench provides potentially useful evaluation of affordance points and visual trajectories. Table 3 includes component ablations: removing SrCoT reduces point accuracy from 61.82% to 26.21% and increases trajectory RMSE from 78.26 to 99.53. Physical-robot demonstrations provide additional evidence of practical feasibility.
weaknesses: The headline simulation result is inconsistent with Table 4. FSD’s four task-success rates are 41.6%, 50.0%, 33.3%, and 37.5%, averaging approximately 40.6%, not 54.1%. With 24 episodes per task, unequal weighting cannot explain this discrepancy. Using the displayed task results, FSD falls below SpatialVLA (FT) at 42.7%, contradicting the claimed best average performance. This materially undermines a central empirical claim.

Zero-shot generalization is insufficiently established. FSD training uses BridgeData, RT-X, and DROID; VABench draws from overlapping dataset families, and simulation evaluates related manipulation tasks. The paper does not document episode-, scene-, object-, or task-level separation sufficiently to distinguish transfer without downstream fine-tuning from generalization to genuinely unseen tasks. Section 3.3 also describes iteratively refining filters against manually annotated test sets without clarifying their separation from final evaluation.

The execution method leaves a crucial geometric gap. Back-projecting a predicted image waypoint using observed depth yields a visible surface point, which need not represent the intended free-space waypoint of a lifted object. The paper does not sufficiently explain how it resolves this ambiguity, determines orientations and clearance, or converts object trajectories into feasible gripper motions. Reliance on GraspNet, predetermined grasp poses, and motion planning also makes controlled executor comparisons important.

Comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed reasoning contribution. The trajectory baseline is a DINOv2 predictor with substantially different pretraining and architecture, while closely related hierarchical methods such as HAMSTER lack direct evaluation. Real-world baselines are restricted to start/end points, disadvantaging them on trajectory-dependent tasks. Table 3 offers useful ablations, but training-budget controls and downstream robot-success ablations are missing.

VABench’s validity needs stronger support. It contains only 300 problems, with limited information about annotation agreement and split composition. Coordinate error against a reference trajectory can penalize alternative valid paths, while GPT-based scoring lacks reported validation against human judgments or physical success. Consequently, improved benchmark scores do not by themselves establish feasible or collision-free execution.

Evaluation uncertainty and reproducibility are inadequate. Real-world trial counts, confidence intervals, detailed success criteria, and failure breakdowns are absent from the supplied manuscript. Simulation baselines are imported from another paper without sufficient protocol reconciliation. Essential training, filtering, execution, and evaluation details are repeatedly deferred to Appendices A–J, which are not included in the supplied 14-page PDF.

Novelty is primarily in combining established components rather than a clearly differentiated technical mechanism. The proposed self-consistency mechanism is described as inverse-task instruction prediction without an explicit cycle-consistency objective. Its trajectory gains are modest, particularly GPT Score changing from 5.45 to 5.49, so claims of its critical contribution require stronger evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses an important robotics problem: transferring visual reasoning into manipulation through embodiment-independent affordance points, boxes, and trajectories. The overall architecture is understandable and practically motivated.

The spatial reasoning evaluation is broad and shows meaningful improvements over the ASMv2 backbone, including CVBench average accuracy of 80.9% versus 66.4%, EmbSpatial accuracy of 63.3% versus 57.4%, and RoboRefIt accuracy of 56.7% versus 48.4%.
The VABench ablations provide positive evidence for spatially grounded reasoning: removing SrCoT reduces point accuracy from 61.82% to 26.21% and increases trajectory RMSE from 78.26 to 99.53.
The automatic annotation pipeline, proposed benchmark, and demonstrations on both simulated and physical robots represent a substantial integration effort with potential practical value.
weaknesses: The headline simulation result is inconsistent with Table 4. FSD's four task success rates—41.6%, 50.0%, 33.3%, and 37.5%—average to approximately 40.6%, not 54.1%. Each task reportedly has 24 episodes, so unequal weighting cannot explain this discrepancy. Based on the listed task results, FSD falls below SpatialVLA (FT) at 42.7%, contradicting the claimed best average performance. This materially undermines a central empirical claim.

The zero-shot generalization claim is insufficiently established. Training uses BridgeData, RT-X, and DROID, while VABench draws from overlapping dataset sources and simulation evaluates related manipulation tasks. Episode, scene, object, and task separation are not documented. Section 3.3 also states that filtering criteria were iteratively refined against manually annotated test sets; whether these are independent of reported evaluation sets must be clarified.

Robot comparisons do not isolate the proposed reasoning method. FSD uses depth, GraspNet or predetermined grasp poses, and motion planning, whereas VLA results are imported from another paper without establishing matched sensing and execution conditions. Physical-robot baselines are restricted to start/end points while FSD can generate trajectories. Matched-controller comparisons and robot-level ablations are needed to attribute gains to SrCoT and alignment.

Essential reproducibility details are deferred to appendices A–J, which are absent from the supplied 14-page manuscript. Missing details include training hyperparameters and data mixtures, filtering and annotation procedures, benchmark scoring prompts, physical-robot trial counts and success criteria, and controller implementation. In particular, depth back-projection alone does not explain how image-space waypoints above surfaces acquire appropriate free-space depths, orientations, and gripper actions.

The trajectory evaluation provides limited evidence of executable manipulation quality. VABench contains only 300 problems, with no clear breakdown or uncertainty estimates. Coordinate error against a reference trajectory can penalize alternative valid paths, while GPT-based scoring is not validated against human judgments or physical success. The only external trajectory baseline is a DINOv2 predictor with substantially different pretraining and architecture; stronger related approaches such as HAMSTER and LLARVA are discussed but not experimentally compared.

The methodological novelty and component contributions remain only partly established. Spatially grounded CoT, hierarchical visual guidance, and inverse-task supervision build closely on existing approaches. There are no controlled ablations of the staged curriculum or data mixture, and the alignment contribution to trajectory GPT Score is only 5.49 versus 5.45 without uncertainty estimates. The available evidence supports a promising system, but not the strength of the paper's broader claims about overcoming data scarcity and embodiment heterogeneity.
